opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about what we're actually asking for. With language models, the reason a foundation model works is that everyone shares the same "schema," so to speak. English is English. Images are pixels. You pretrain on the internet and the structure of the data you see at inference time is basically the structure you saw during training.

Enterprise data is completely different. Every company has its own database: its own tables, its own columns, its own way of linking customers to transactions to products to support tickets. One retailer's schema looks nothing like another's, and neither looks like a bank's or a hospital's. So the idea that you could train a single model, show it a database it has never seen before, with tables and column names it has never encountered, and have it make accurate predictions about, say, which customer is going to churn or what someone will buy next, without any training on that specific data, sounds almost absurd. Traditionally that's months of work: a data scientist joins tables, engineers hundreds of features, trains a model, tunes it, and does that again for every new task.

What changed my mind is realizing that underneath all that heterogeneity there's a common structure. A relational database is really a graph: rows are entities, primary and foreign keys are the edges, and timestamps give you the temporal dynamics. Once you represent the data that way, the patterns that matter turn out to be surprisingly universal. Things like recency, frequency, how your neighbors behave, how activity propagates through connected entities. Those patterns recur across domains. So if you pretrain a graph transformer over many diverse relational datasets, it learns to reason over that structure in context, much the way an LLM learns to reason over text.

That's why it felt outlandish, and why it's so exciting that it works. You point the model at a new database, specify the prediction task, and it gives you a prediction that's competitive with, and often better than, a model a team spent weeks hand-building. And if you then fine-tune on that specific database, you get further gains on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response says it seems almost absurd that a model could predict on an unseen database without training on that data, because each company’s schema and relationships differ. This clearly challenges how learned structure could transfer to an unfamiliar use case.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, if you think about it, it really is kind of outlandish, right? Think about what we're actually proposing. You have a company with a database they've been building for years. Dozens, maybe hundreds of tables. Customers, transactions, products, support tickets, whatever it is. Their own column names, their own schema, their own quirks, their own business logic baked into how the data is structured. Nobody outside that company has ever seen this data. The model has certainly never seen it.

And now the claim is: you take a model that was pretrained somewhere else, on entirely different databases, you point it at this new database, and without any training, without any feature engineering, without a data scientist spending six months building a pipeline, you say "predict which of these customers will churn next month" or "predict the lifetime value of this user," and it just... works. It gives you a good prediction.

If you had told me that five years ago, I would have said that's not how machine learning on tabular data works. The entire history of enterprise ML is that every problem is its own project. You hire people, they understand the schema, they hand-craft features, they join tables, they aggregate, they train a model, and that model is useless on the next company's data. It's completely bespoke.

So the reason I say it's almost outlandish is that it's exactly the thing the field had basically accepted as impossible, or at least as not the way things are done. And what made it possible is really the same thing that happened with language. In language, you had the same argument: every NLP task used to be its own model. Then foundation models came along and the whole thing collapsed into one model that generalizes. What we figured out is that relational data, databases, actually have enough shared structure across companies, the way entities link to each other, the way events happen over time, that you can learn that structure once and transfer it. The specific column names don't matter. The underlying relational patterns do.

But even having built it, when I see it work on a database it's never encountered, I still find it a little bit surprising. It feels like it shouldn't be possible, and yet it is.

r001.rationale: The response calls prediction on a never-seen company database without training or feature engineering “outlandish,” then explains the surprising premise: shared relational patterns across databases can transfer to unfamiliar prediction tasks.

astra-6.text:
Because every business has its own way of organizing data. You have different tables, different columns, different relationships, and the meaning of those things changes from one company to another. So the idea that you could take a model, show it a database it has never seen before, and ask it to make useful predictions—that’s a pretty remarkable proposition.

With language, there is a shared structure. We all use words, and those words carry meaning across documents. With business data, even figuring out what a row represents and how it connects to other information is part of the problem. And then you have to understand the prediction task: Are we predicting whether a customer will leave? Whether an invoice will be paid? What someone will buy next?

Traditionally, you would build a specific machine-learning pipeline for each of those tasks. You would work with someone who understands the data, construct features, and train a model. A foundation model is effectively promising to transfer enough knowledge across these very different settings to do something useful on a new one. That’s what makes the idea seem almost outlandish.

r001.rationale: The response explains that business data structures, meanings, and prediction tasks vary across companies, making transfer to unfamiliar data remarkable. It does not clearly challenge the idea that learning relationships among business numbers alone could enable those predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
Because every business has its own data, organized in its own way. You might have a database with hundreds of tables, different columns, different relationships, and you want to predict something very specific: Which customer will churn? Which product will somebody buy next?

Traditionally, you would need someone to understand that database, build features, and train a model for that particular task. So the idea that you could take a model, bring it to a database it has never seen before, and have it make useful predictions—that’s a pretty remarkable proposition. It has to generalize across different schemas, different meanings of the data, and different prediction tasks. What is the common structure that lets it do that? That’s the fascinating question.

r001.rationale: The response calls prediction on an unseen database remarkable and asks what common structure enables generalization, but it does not specifically challenge whether learning relationships among business numbers alone could support an unfamiliar use case.
